newsitem.title: USA: U.S. tries to have it both ways on dollar.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tries to have it both ways on dollar.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The United States seems to be trying to have it both ways when it comes to the dollar and, perhaps not surprisingly, the currency market does not quite know what to make of it.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated on Thursday that a strong dollar was in America's interest. But, in virtually the same breath, he voiced concern about the weakness of the Japanese yen against the U.S. currency.

The dollar jumped in the immediate wake of Rubin's remarks, as currency traders concluded that the United States would not do anything to stop the currency's continued advance. But it fell back later amid fears that Japan at least would try to check its rise by selling dollars.

The dollar ended Thursday at 125.85 Japanese yen and 1.7190 German marks, off from 126.80 yen and 1.7255 marks on Wednesday. It temporarily touched a 4-1/2-year high vs. the yen in Tokyo before being hit by a barrage of comments by Japanese officials.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told bank executives in Tokyo on Thursday that the yen's recent weakness against the dollar had been excessive.
Japan is worried that the yen's fall will bloat its surplus, risking trade friction with the United States.
The weakness of the yen -- it has dropped 60 percent against the dollar over the past two years -- makes Japanese exports more competitive on world markets.

"We share the concern expressed by the Japanese authorities last night about recent movements in the yen because of the impact on Japan's external (trade) surplus," Rubin said in a statement on Thursday.
David Gilmore, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics, said that both countries seemed to be signalling that they believe the dollar has risen too far against the yen.
"The dollar is a little bit too high for either country's liking," Gilmore said, adding, "They want to stabilise the situation but the market hasn't really paid much attention."
Several analysts said they see the dollar pushing higher against the yen in the coming weeks, despite the concern voiced on Thursday by Japan and the United States.

With interest rates in Japan low and those in the United States high and possibly heading higher, the demand for dollars from Japanese investors is solid, said David Hale, chief economist at Zurich Kemper Investments in Chicago.
Gilmore said it will probably take dollar-selling intervention by the United States and Japan and a change in the economic fundamentals to turn the dollar around.
"I think it keeps going up until it ultimately draws out intervention," he said, adding, "In order to impress currency traders, Treasury is going to have to sell some dollars."
Japanese officials hinted on Thursday that they might be ready to step into the currency market to sell dollars.

Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara told Reuters in Japan that intervention in foreign exchange markets was possible if exchange rates deviated greatly from economic fundamentals. He added that he did not think recent currency movements were in line with those fundamentals.
Interviewed on CNBC television, Rubin declined to comment on the possibility of intervention, but to some traders his comments seemed to suggest that such a move was not imminent.

"Our policy on the dollar is unchanged," Rubin said in a separate statement. "Over time, exchange rates generally reflect fundamentals and the fundamentals of the U.S. economy have been relatively strong for the past four years."
During his more than two years as Treasury chief, Rubin has been a tireless proponent of the benefits of a strong dollar because it keeps interest rates and inflation down.
The United States last intervened in the foreign exchange market in the third quarter of 1995, when it was a buyer of dollars.
